We demonstrate that a heightened version of Godel's first incompleteness theorem, which was independently devised by Sokal and Rosser, results in a more substantial conclusion concerning any formal, axiomatic theory that is capable of counting and possesses a specific level of mathematical sophistication. In such a theory, no formalizable "truth predicate" can be developed, which enables the proof of a plethora of non-obvious statements of logical interest.

This study expands on Hadamard's three circles theorem by introducing a functional interpretation using monogenic functions in higher dimensions. The original proof reveals that Hadamard's theorem can be viewed as a specific result of the properties of monogenic functions, specifically the Cauchy-type formulas and the uniqueness theorem. The connection allows us to generalize Hadamard's theorem within the context of real-valued functions that are real-part expressions of monogenic functions in higher dimensions. The latter includes a generalized version of the three circles theorem.

Imaging the unknown medium properties in stochastic linear scalar hyperbolic equations proves to be challenging due to the ill-posed problem. This challenge is exacerbated by added noise in measurement data. To compensate for this difficulty, a novel conditional Wasserstein GAN called the regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN is proposed. This model generates posterior samples that are conditioned on the measured data and produced probabilities. The introduction of a regularized term in the Wasserstein GAN objective function ensures that the generated posterior distributions match the exact posterior distribution up to a certain L2 distance. As a result, this model is guaranteed to produce posterior samples that are close to the exact posterior distribution. This efficacy is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted in recent studies on imaging and resolution of partial differential equations, where generated images were verified to be indistinguishable from exact images posterior to L2 distance normalization.

This research paper examines linear time-invariant systems that employ fractional-order operators and include subspaces that behave identically under system transformations. The aim of the study is to establish invariance properties in these complex systems. The key finding reveals that a linear subspace is insensitive to system dynamics if it satisfies a specific non-homogeneous condition, which can be evaluated efficiently using a linear system of equations. The paper also investigates the invariance of subspaces in fractional-order polynomial systems, Kalman filters, and optimal control applications, providing concise mathematical representations and feasible computational strategies.

Researchers studied PSR B1133+16, a pulsar with a relatively long rotation period, by analyzing radio observations spanning nearly five decades. By splitting its emission into individual scattering events, scientists isolated numerous screen interfaces along the pulsar's light path. As a notable finding, a significant distance of approximately 6 kpc was determined for Earth in relation to the pulsar, a value confirmed through wideband substructure analysis and validated by other methods. Furthermore, a detailed examination of scattering properties was performed to calculate the pulsar's interstellar environment.

Using a cascaded network structure, a frequency-domain adaptive algorithm for speech signal processing is proposed. This algorithm applies the frequency-domain adaptive algorithm in each stage of the cascaded network. The proposed method enhances the modeling of quasi-periodic signals like speech by reducing sidelobe interferences. The frequency-domain adaptive algorithm in each stage of the cascaded network is based on the normalized least mean square algorithm and the recursive least square algorithm. The proposed method's performance is evaluated and compared to other algorithms. The results show that the cascaded network structure significantly reduces sidelobe interferences. The frequency-domain adaptive algorithm based on the normalized least mean square algorithm outperforms the recursive least square algorithm in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. The optimal time delay of the algorithms is investigated. The proposed method's performance is influenced by its order of the cascaded network.

We introduce a concept called labeller that allows us to generate invariants for certain bicategorical constructions, subsequently using these invariants to recreate topological Hochschild homology through a reduced formula involving shadows. This shadow-based representation of thh(B) is specifically demonstrated using the example of the topological K-theory of gluable spaces, ultimately leading to the derivation of an analytic interpretation for the HH(shthh(B)) in-set *-category.

VGG-Sound Source is a comprehensive audio source reconstruction dataset created from the VGG-Sound dataset, an extensive collection of 1.5 million labeled sound clips from YouTube videos. With over 60 seconds of training data and 11 diverse categories, VGG-SS sets a new standard for source reconstruction benchmarks, surpassing existing datasets in size and diversity. These benchmarks feature high-quality target sounds and source masks, produced using a multi-condition convolutional neural network, which yields superior results compared to conventional approaches. VGG-SS is accompanied by three evaluation metrics, including source separation quality, target sound preservation, and mask estimation accuracy, and showcases significant performance improvements in source reconstruction, particularly when trained on large datasets. The code and dataset are available for public use at: https://github.com/vgg/SS-Reconstruction.

To tackle the challenge of representing high-dimensional node features in small-dimensional spaces, we introduce the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN). LGCN surpasses current hyperbolic GCNs in node feature representation, with our model also adapting easily to other non-Euclidean spaces like spherical spaces. The core component of LGCN is a novel Lorentzian graph convolutional layer, which separates dependent and independent components of node features to achieve invariance and independence, and thereby reduces dimensionality. The proposed model is evaluated in multiple scenarios, including homogeneous and inhomogeneous graphs, and our results show that LGCN outperforms existing methods. Additionally, we leverage the Lorentzian graph convolutional layer to model spherical spherical spaces and achieve state-of-the-art performance on two benchmark datasets.

This study focuses on finding a stable approximation to the domain of a scalar linear elliptic partial differential equation (PDE) given incomplete boundary data and additional measurements taken within the unknown domain. Following this, the findings are extended to demonstrate that, under specific conditions, incorporating observability inequalities yields stability results for certain inverse problems involving PDEs. A natural extension of this stability property is then established for a class of boundary value problems formulated over general compact manifolds. The proof of this extended stability property relies on the Carleman estimate, a particular type of observability inequality. The paper also introduces a stable numerical method to approximate the unknown domain by formulating a regularized optimization problem. Theoretical proof of the convergence of this solver is provided, along with the rate of convergence being estimated numerically in a subsequent numerical experiment.

The Tsallis distribution can be reinterpreted through the lens of random walks in configurable spaces, uncovering its broader applicability to social systems governed by choice rules. This transformation also provides a probabilistic framework, offering useful insights and unanticipated benefits, as seen in the case of studying information flow in preference hierarchies.

The inclusion of a mass term in gravitational perturbations typically results in an undesirable increase in the number of free parameters, potentially leading to an infinite number of new physical degrees of freedom. The proposed Fierz-Pauli-like approach, however, demonstrates that this unwanted outcome can be avoided and provides a distinct scenario for massive gravity, distinguished from the well-known de Rham-Gullstrand approach by a fundamental difference in symmetry. The proposed theory also offers multiple possible interpretations of the mass scale, primarily driven by the choice of metric sign parameter, and this theory can be applied to either of two possible fundamental geometry concepts, either metric-dependent or metric-independent. For classical and quantum systems, the concept of Hamiltonian dynamics is similarly defined using symplectic transformations. However, due to the ambiguity in defining the inverse of quantum dynamics, various Hamiltonian dynamics scenarios emerge in quantum mechanics. In this study, we classify four types of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics: inverse dynamics is defined unambiguously; inverse dynamics has multiple interpretations; the quantum class involves Hamiltonian dynamics; and classical mechanics is the guiding principle. Each subset is organized based on system complexity, represented by Wigner function negativity, steering, and quantum correlation generation under random Hamiltonian evolution.

A common analogy for illustrating negative temperature involves a hypothetical two-level system similar to a spin-1/2 particle, where temperature is represented by population differences between energy levels. In this analogy, a system can have a negative temperature if it's more populated at the higher energy level. Although this analogy might seem intuitive, it's not universally applicable and can lead to misleading conclusions, especially when generalized to multi-level systems. Here, we show that the two-level system analogy incorrectly implies that a state with a negative definite temperature matrix necessarily has a negative total temperature. To avoid confusion, we recommend against using the term "negative total temperature" and suggest alternative language to describe specific thermal properties, rather than relying on the two-level system analogy.

We incorporate a minimal dark sector into a type of seesaw framework known as dark parity, which incorporates a minimal dark parity symmetry to explain the dark matter paradox. The minimal dark sector is represented by two scalar fields and is shown to maintain dark parity symmetry. However, due to the incorporation of a minimal dark parity, the vacuum stability is placed at risk. To rectify this issue, we propose two distinct scenarios: the first involves adding a natural charger to one of the scalar fields, which results in the field becoming tachyonic in nature; the second scenario necessitates the incorporation of either a tachyonic field or a negative mass term for one of the dark sector fields. Both of these scenarios break dark parity symmetry, thereby ensuring the stability of the vacuum.

Researchers often represent the spin-orbit effect, electron interaction, and crystal field splitting using approximate methods, but these individual effects can't be disentangled in real-world situations. Instead, they concurrently influence the energy spectra of transition metal oxides, so it's more precise to study them together as a single, unified quantity - the tensor of electron interactions. This approach has already been successfully applied and measured directly, using x-ray scattering, at the interface of Sr$_{x}$Ca$_{1-x}$Mn$_{7/8}$As$_{7/8}$, a system known for its unusual spin physics and absence of long-range magnetic ordering. By analyzing this data using a unique method called the Bethe-Salpeter equation, scientists uncovered the detailed structure of the tensor of electron interactions, and how it changes in response to small variations in chemical composition. Notably, the effective spin-orbit effect appears in this system, despite lacking any direct influence from spin-orbit interaction itself. By studying this interplay of effects in this unusual system, researchers have paved the way for a deeper understanding of its unusual spin properties and lack of long-range magnetic ordering.

This research explores the relationship between relative $I$-functions of smooth toric complete intersections from a particular family, characterized by having divisors that are smooth within given loci. We establish a crucial property: the ratio of two relative $I$-functions is equal to the product of two $s$-coefficients, derived from their defining equations. This ratio also represents the product of two factors, each corresponding to the holomorphic integral along a specific circle in toric loci. Moreover, we establish that these ratios yield a consistent and meaningful extension of Kohlhaase's and Miller's findings regarding toric hypersurfaces and arrangements of hyperplanes.

A significant issue with generative adversarial networks is their inability to control the
generated images through the latent code, which limits their applicability in
medical imaging, particularly in analyzing sick patients. Our study introduces Latent
Dynamics Evaluation (LDE), a metric that assesses a model's capacity to adhere to
the temporal characteristics present in images. We demonstrate LDE's utility in
evaluating generative models capable of processing time series images, including
medical scans. Our findings show that models performing well in time series
generation tasks, including MRI sequencing and respiratory phase synthesis
using PET scans, are highly correlated with LDE scores. Furthermore, our study
shows that LDE can be used in a collaborative embedding framework to extract
features from the latent code that directly correlates with clinical information.

A common challenge in data analysis occurs when working with high-dimensional data, where visualizing information for typical users who aren't technically savvy is complicated due to the high visualization difficulty above a 3D dimension.  Expert systems like GEL-Vis and DimensionQuest require users to provide multiple parameters and have limited flexibility in customizing graphics.  Our proposed method, ViDaExpert, is a user-friendly, interactive tool designed to meet the needs of experts and researchers in visualizing high-dimensional data using Elbow clustering.  With ViDaExpert, users can easily visualize data in any dimension, with options to adjust the method used to identify natural groupings and customize the appearance of the graph.  The system is particularly suited for analyzing and visualizing datasets with unusual shapes, as seen in our test cases using real-world datasets, including MNIST and the Iris flower dataset.
